vignette:
He is 58, an African man who has spent most of his adult life standing behind a salon chair, talking gently over the hum of clippers and the smell of hair oil. Before the robbery, he is known by customers as steady and warm, the kind of hairdresser who remembers the names of their children and notices when someone has had a difficult week. He works long days and comes home tired but satisfied, carrying himself with the quiet pride of a man who has built something dependable. He lives with his wife, and their life together is ordinary in ways that matter to him: evening tea, shared complaints about rising costs, church on Sundays, calls from relatives back home.

The robbery happens on a weekday evening after he closes the salon. He is later than usual because a regular customer comes in just before closing, asking for "only a quick trim." By the time he counts the cash and pulls down the shutter, the street is mostly empty. He notices two young men near the corner but thinks little of it at first. As he walks to his car with the day's earnings tucked into a worn leather bag, they move toward him quickly. One grabs his shoulder from behind. The other stands in front of him and demands the bag. At first he is confused, almost irritated, as if this is some misunderstanding. Then he sees the knife.

What stays with him is not only the fear but the humiliation. He hears himself pleading. He hands over the bag, but one of them shoves him hard enough that he falls against the side of the car. His cheek hits metal, and for a moment all he can hear is the pounding in his ears. The men run. He does not chase them. He slides down onto the pavement and sits there, stunned, ashamed of how weak he suddenly feels. When he reaches home, his wife opens the door and immediately sees blood near his mouth. He tells her, "They took it, all of it," but what he means is not just the money.

In the first days afterward, he sleeps very little. He closes his eyes and sees the knife again, bright and close. He startles at footsteps outside the house. When his wife reaches for him in bed, he jerks before he recognizes her. He keeps replaying the moment when he noticed the two young men and did nothing. He tells himself he should have crossed the street, should have asked someone to walk him out, should have closed earlier. During the day, he drifts in and out of the memory without warning. A customer laughing too loudly, the jangle of keys, young men gathering near the bus stop-each one sends a flash of panic through him.

He returns to work because he cannot afford not to, but the salon no longer feels safe. He used to enjoy the last appointment of the day; now he watches the clock anxiously if a customer is still in the chair near closing time. He checks the lock again and again. If someone lingers outside the front window, his hands begin to shake so badly he has to set down the scissors. He becomes careful in ways that look, at first glance, like practicality. He stops carrying cash. He asks his wife to call when he is about to leave work. He parks only under bright lights. But the caution grows into something bigger. He avoids walking alone, avoids unfamiliar customers, avoids the whole side street where it happened. When business is slow, he feels relief; when it is busy, he feels trapped.

His wife says he is no longer with her even when he is sitting beside her. He knows what she means. At dinner, he stares past her shoulder, listening for sounds outside. At church, he chooses the seat nearest the exit. He used to joke easily with clients, but now his patience is thin. If someone comes up behind him unexpectedly, anger shoots through him before he can control it. He hates this version of himself. He especially hates what it has done to his work. Hairdressing has always required closeness-hands near faces, trust, easy conversation. Now even ordinary interactions feel effortful. He notices young male customers make him tense. He feels guilty for that, then disgusted with himself.

At night he sometimes dreams that he is back outside the salon, unable to move, his bag still in his hand, his body refusing to run. Other nights he wakes certain that someone is in the house. He gets up and checks every window, every lock, then lies awake until dawn. He is exhausted, but sleep feels dangerous. His wife tells him he cries out in his dreams. He denies it at first, then admits he is afraid to sleep because in the dream he feels again the exact moment when the knife appears and the world narrows to survival.

Months later, he speaks about the robbery as if it happened both yesterday and in another lifetime. He says the money was replaceable, but something in him has remained on that pavement outside the salon. He still goes to work, still stands behind the chair, still greets customers with politeness. From a distance, his life appears intact. Up close, nearly every part of his day is organized around fear-avoiding, checking, scanning, bracing. He says he misses being relaxed in his own body. What troubles him most is that he no longer trusts the ordinary world that once felt familiar: a quiet street, a stranger approaching, the end of a workday, the simple act of walking to his car.
